transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, to be perfectly honest, I’m not entirely sure where to begin, because... well, it’s one of those things that just sort of creeps up on you, you know? I’ve been a secondary school teacher for over thirty years now—I have my master's, I love my students, I really do—but I’ve been having this ridiculous issue where I just... I cannot seem to stay in my chair. It’s what finally made me make this appointment, actually. 

I just keep getting up. Like, in the middle of our departmental meetings, or even just sitting at dinner when everyone else is perfectly content being seated. I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I just feel this intense need to move, so I’ll invent a reason. I'll tell myself I suddenly need to refill my coffee—even if my cup is practically full—or I'll get up to check a handout on the front table that I already read, or I'll just walk all the way to the back of the room to stand. 

It’s not like anything is actually urgent! I mean, nothing is happening that requires me to be up. And like I said, it’s not just at school, it’s at home, too. We had the neighbors over for dinner last weekend, a lovely couple, we made a beautiful roast, and I think I must have popped up from the dining table five or six times while everyone else was just sitting and enjoying their meal. My husband finally gave me this look, and I realized how disruptive it must seem, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it.
When you're sitting down, before you get up, are you having difficulty concentrating on what's happening around you, or does your mind feel like it's racing?

Well, no, actually... it’s not really like that at all. I mean, you’d think so, wouldn't you? That I must be lost in thought or completely distracted to be popping up out of my chair like that, but I’m really not. My mind doesn't feel like it's racing—it's actually quite clear, usually. And I’m paying perfect attention to whatever is going on around me. 

Take that dinner party I just mentioned, for example. We were talking with the neighbors—the Hendersons, they live just across the street and have this absolutely stunning garden—and David Henderson was right in the middle of explaining how he overwinters his dahlias. Which is something I’ve actually been trying to learn about, because mine always seem to rot in the basement no matter what I do. So I was hanging on his every word, completely focused on what he was saying. I wasn't distracted in the slightest! But even while I was listening so intently, taking it all in, I just... I still had to stand up. I ended up standing over by the sideboard, just nodding along to his gardening advice. 

And it’s the exact same thing at school during our curriculum meetings. The head of the department will be going over the new reading list for the upperclassmen, and I’m taking notes, I’m fully engaged, my brain is right there in the room. I'm not daydreaming or jumping from thought to thought. It’s just... it’s just my body that seems to want to be somewhere else, not my mind. Does that make sense? Because I know it sounds a bit contradictory, being so perfectly focused on a conversation but still feeling this bizarre compulsion to go stand at the back of the room while it's happening.
How long has this problem with needing to get up and move around been going on? Did you experience similar difficulties as a child or teenager, or is this something that has developed more recently?

Well, as for when I was younger, a child or a teenager... I mean, I was always a busy person, but I certainly wasn't popping up out of my seat during a dinner party or a class like I am now. This specific issue, this... this absolute inability to just stay put, it’s really become noticeably harder to manage much more recently. I'd say it’s been about eight months. Yes, right around eight months. 

And I know exactly why that timeline sticks in my head, because that’s right when my youngest left for college. You know, when you have kids in the house, there is always a certain level of activity. You're always moving, always doing something, checking on them, doing laundry, cooking, running around. But then they pack up and move out, and suddenly... the house just became so quiet. My husband and I were officially empty nesters. And you'd think I would finally just sit down and relax, wouldn't you? Enjoy the peace and quiet after all those years of running around. 

But it was almost like the quieter the house got, the more restless my body got. Without the natural busyness of having my youngest there to keep me on my feet, I found myself having to just invent reasons to get up. It’s been about eight months of this quiet house, and eight months of me just absolutely failing to sit still in it. I just can't seem to settle into the stillness, if that makes sense. It's just so strange how a change in your environment like that can bring something out, isn't it? Because before they left, I really don't remember it being this much of an issue, or at least it wasn't something I noticed because I was always supposed to be up and doing something anyway, but now with the house being so quiet... I just don't know what to do with myself.

Before your youngest left for college, even if you didn't think much about it at the time, do you remember ever having periods where you felt restless or found it difficult to sit still for extended periods?

Well, now that you frame it quite like that... I suppose... I mean, I know I just said a moment ago that I wasn't popping up out of my seat when I was younger, and that's true for my teenage years and early adulthood, but... if I really think back, I mean way, way back... 

It’s actually rather funny you bring it up, because it reminds me of something my mother used to say. Bless her, she kept absolutely everything, every scrap of paper from my childhood in this massive, expanding green folder. And my report cards, even from when I was just a little girl, they were always so incredibly consistent. The teachers would always write that I was a very bright student, very capable and eager to learn, but... but that I simply could not stay in my seat. That, and that I had a terrible time waiting my turn. 

My mother used to joke about it constantly at family gatherings. She would tell my aunts and uncles that she was surprised the school didn't make her pay for floor repairs, because she swore I must have worn a literal path into the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! 

And it's true, I was always, always getting up to sharpen my pencil. It was just a manual one, you know, the crank kind attached to the wall by the chalkboard, and I would be up there three, four times a lesson. I suppose a dull pencil was just the perfect excuse to get out of my chair, wasn't it? Just like pretending I need to refill my coffee cup at my departmental meetings now! 

So, I guess... yes, if I really sit and reflect on it, that restless feeling, that physical urge to just get up and move, it must have been there when I was a child, too. I just hadn't put two and two together because, well, you just think of it as being an energetic little girl, don't you? You don't think of it as a pattern that’s going to follow you all the way into your sixties! But those report cards... oh, they were quite clear about my inability to just stay put. I hadn't thought about that pencil sharpener in years, but yes, I suppose I have always found it a bit of a trial to just sit still for long stretches.
